analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans legally buy cheaper prescription drugs from approved Canadian pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill had 9 cosponsors from both parties but never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Health and Human Services Department to write rules, within 180 days, letting individuals import up to a 90-day supply of a prescription drug from a Canadian pharmacy approved and listed by the government. The drug must match an FDA-approved drug in active ingredient, dose, and form, must be filled with a valid US prescription, and cannot be resold. Controlled substances, biological products like insulin-type biotech drugs, IV drugs, and drugs needing refrigeration would be excluded. Pharmacies would have to be licensed in Canada, at least five years old, and pass quality-assurance and testing criteria.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay high out-of-pocket prices for prescription drugs, especially people without insurance or with high deductibles. Because US brand-name drugs routinely cost far more than the identical drugs sold in Canada, personal importation lets people buy the same medicine at the lower Canadian price. Studies and prior versions of this idea estimate large per-person savings on common maintenance drugs.

how_it_helps.text: Allows individuals to import up to a 90-day personal supply of a prescription drug from a government-approved Canadian pharmacy, filled with a valid US prescription [S2].

Requires the drug to have the same active ingredients, dosage form, route of administration, and strength as the FDA-approved version of the drug, and bars reselling, so imports stay personal-use [S3].

Excludes the highest-risk products — controlled substances, biological products, IV and infused drugs, and refrigerated drugs — and requires HHS to certify and publish a list of approved Canadian pharmacies with quality-assurance and product-testing requirements [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would lose sales in the US market when customers buy the identical drugs at Canadian prices, roughly 30-70% lower for many common drugs. US pharmacies could also lose some prescription business. Taxpayers pay nothing; the bill has no public spending attached.

drawbacks.text: The FDA has long warned that drugs sold abroad are not always made or stored under US standards; even with certification requirements, personal importation carries some risk of counterfeit, expired, or improperly handled medicine slipping through [S2].

The bill excludes biological products — the fastest-growing and most expensive category of drugs — and limits imports to personal use, so it lowers costs for individuals who use it but does nothing to change drug prices for the health system as a whole [S2].
Canada's domestic market is too small to supply US demand if importation became widespread, a practical constraint critics of importation plans raise.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For an individual patient, the upside is concrete: the same pill bought in Canada often costs a fraction of the US price, and the bill's screening rules exclude the riskiest product categories. The honest objections are that no safety screening is airtight for medicine bought across a border, and that personal importation is a work-around rather than a fix for US drug pricing — it helps the people who find the program, not the system. Still, the potential savings for people who struggle to afford prescriptions are substantial and the exclusions were a genuine attempt to manage the safety risk.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee on day one, and nothing ever happened to it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chellie Pingree introduced the bill on March 9, 2017, joined by nine cosponsors, five Democrats and four Republicans [S4].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the next day to that committee's Health Subcommittee [S5].
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, who kept the US market free of Canadian price competition. Americans who could not afford their prescriptions gained nothing from the two years the bill sat untouched in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was split 5 Democrats and 4 Republicans, but the bill never reached a vote, so the full partisan shape of support and opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill lets Americans buy the identical drugs at Canadian prices, which run far below US list prices, cutting into US sales of patented medicines. Keeping personal importation off the books protects that price gap, which is why drug-importation bills have repeatedly died without a vote despite bipartisan interest.

industries.industry: Canadian pharmacies, including online mail-order pharmacies
industries.note: Certified Canadian pharmacies would gain a legal channel to sell to US customers for personal use. Their interest here runs alongside patients', since both sides benefit from the sale happening.
Some prescription volume would shift to Canadian sources, costing US pharmacies dispensing revenue, though the 90-day personal-use limit keeps the shift modest.
